content: Heroic medicine refers to aggressive medical practices or treatment methods that were commonly used in the past but were later replaced by more scientifically advanced approaches. The origin of the term heroic medicine is unclear, but it is believed to have been first used by American or British scholars studying the history of medicine in the early 20th century. This form of medicine, where the patient was considered heroic for enduring the treatments rather than the physician or the therapy itself, was prevalent between the 1780s and 1850s. Benjamin Rush, a signer of the American Declaration of Independence and one of the founding figures of American medicine, was a prominent advocate of heroic medicine. Rush, who had received his medical training at Edinburgh University between 1766 and 1768, strongly supported these aggressive therapeutic methods. During the so-called Age of Heroic Medicine (1780–1850), educated professional physicians employed highly aggressive treatments. These included bloodletting (venesection), intestinal purging using substances like calomel (a mercury-based compound), inducing vomiting with tartar emetic, promoting excessive sweating with diaphoretics, and applying blistering agents to the skin. Physicians also treated diseases such as syphilis with mercury-based salves. Although these treatments were often well-intentioned and widely accepted by the medical community of the time, they were ultimately harmful to patients.
